title: Hello, World!
objective: Use console.log() and string literals to produce exact text output.

sourceAlignment.title: JavaScript Crash Course
sourceAlignment.author: Nick Morgan
sourceAlignment.note: Adapted for Code Forge's in-browser runtime — no local installation. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: console.log() is a function: a named, reusable action. You call it by writing its name followed by parentheses, and you hand it the thing you want it to display by placing that value inside the parentheses.

Text values in JavaScript are called strings, and you can write them with single quotes, double quotes, or backticks — all three work for a plain string, as long as the opening and closing mark match. Anything inside the quotes is printed exactly as written, including spaces and punctuation.

Programmers traditionally write a tiny program that prints Hello, World! as the first thing they run in a new language. It confirms two things at once: the code runs, and you know how to produce output.
explanation.rule: console.log("some text") outputs the exact text inside the quotes, followed by a new line.

examples.title: Two Ways to Quote
examples.code:
console.log('Single quotes work.');
console.log("So do double quotes.");
examples.note: Single and double quotes both create the same kind of string. Pick one style and be consistent.

checks.question: Which of these is NOT a valid way to write a plain JavaScript string?

feedback.correct: Correct — slashes create a regular expression, not a string. Single quotes, double quotes, and backticks all create strings.
feedback.incorrect: Single quotes, double quotes, and backticks all create strings. Slashes create something else entirely — a regular expression.

assignment.title: Hello, Forge!
assignment.brief: Write greetForge() that logs exactly: Hello, Forge!
requirements: The logged text must be exactly: Hello, Forge!

hints: console.log() prints whatever string you give it.
The exact text is: Hello, Forge! — comma after Hello, exclamation point at the end.
Use either single or double quotes to wrap the text.
Don't forget to call greetForge(); after defining it.
